blocks.text: Recovery technique is Gotō's theoretical system: side-effect countering, the psychological part, and the theory of suicide. It tries to answer one question — after od, how do you get back to a state where you can live normally even without taking the drug.
The Psychological Part: Symptoms Point to Causes

A symptom may not point to a disease, but it will absolutely point to a cause. A cause comes either from past memory or from one's own imagination. To satisfy the desire behind the cause, the neurotic symptom appears: in the unconscious, the symptom is a solution decided after careful thought. The patient always gets some benefit from the neurotic symptom, and that benefit happens to suppress the emergence of the cause.

For example, a patient keeps hitting walls in social situations; to satisfy the desire 'don't get hurt in social situations', the unconscious screens out overly violent symptoms like depression and depersonalization and produces social anxiety. Not daring to go out after fearing social situations brings a huge benefit: there is no social situation at all, so the cause won't appear either.
As long as the psychological cause remains unresolved, ignoring it doesn't just fail to solve the problem; it can evolve into depersonalization.

Anxiety divides into three kinds: realistic anxiety (external, from real danger, useful for avoidance), moral anxiety (internal, from the superego, guilt and shame), and neurotic anxiety (internal, apprehension of some danger). Realistic and moral anxiety are both necessary; only neurotic anxiety seems always to trouble people. But the fact that anxiety exists proves it played some role at some past moment, and points straight at a cause.

Dissociation can dissociate away realistic and moral anxiety, but neurotic anxiety doesn't stop: the dissociated person often lacks the first two yet keeps having neurotic anxiety, and because perception and cognition have dropped, doesn't know where it comes from — anxiety that was already 'floating in the air' becomes even harder to trace under dissociation. Anti-dissociation can strengthen realistic and moral anxiety and strengthen perception, letting a person perceive anxiety more; the upside is that anti-dissociated people can usually locate the source of the anxiety accurately.

The four-square of depression: psychological/physiological × exogenous/endogenous. The cause of psychological depression is psychological, not physiological; exercise therapy and drugs can't cure psychological content; drugs mainly treat physiological depression and assist psychotherapy. This explains why the older generation thinks 'run more, exercise more' will solve depression — that points at a physiological cause and solves physiological depression; thinking 'you're depressed because you have too much free time' makes the mistake of not distinguishing the psychological from the physiological.

The vicious cycle of dissociative disorder/depersonalization: dissociation keeps a person from perceiving the cause, not knowing the source means not being able to solve the cause, and not solving the cause keeps producing dissociation. Solving the cause is the real answer; if you can guarantee a real solution, adding an anti-dissociative alongside is a better choice; giving the patient safe protection is also paramount.

Mania: the death drive turned outward. Depression easily leads to self-harm, mania easily leads to harming others, so forcibly controlling a manic person is necessary. Schizophrenia: the hardest to reach; patients who get this far usually have the most powerful psychological or physiological causes; the elements in their hallucinations often have high analytical value, like dream interpretation.
The Theory of Suicide

When a patient is tortured to the end by the mass of mental illness above, the patient often ends with suicide, because suicide is the one road each person can choose for themselves, and an extremely convenient one. In the patient's view, no matter how big the predicament, it can end in suicide. But this is like the First World War: the war to end all wars ended nothing, and changed the world forever.

Suicide happens because of a predicament that's hard to escape, so help from others is needed to solve it. When the patient has solved the predicament there are often still obsessive ideas left, and then psychological counselling is needed, telling the patient where those ideas come from. Dissociation can break such ideas, and dissociatives can be used when the idea is stubborn — this may also be where ketamine's antidepressant effect comes from.
It may also be about getting some emotional care.
The Neurosis Dextro Causes: Superego Censorship

The user wants to od, but the superego censors, screens out the intent to od, produces meaningless neurotic anxiety, and nausea appears. The user starts vomiting, because the subconscious believes 'if I vomit, then I've o'd', and so comforts itself. Now the neurosis shows: headache, cough — the subconscious believes 'I have a headache and a cough, taking dextro will make me feel better; I'm not o-ing, I'm making myself feel better', and the intent shifts from 'od' to 'make myself feel better', dodging the superego's censorship and letting the person swallow handful after handful of Umi.

The solution is fairly simple: when you have a headache, cough, vomiting or nausea, tell yourself — 'I'm not od-ing badly, I fucking want to od, and the headache and cough and vomiting are all useless'.
The Boundary

The endpoint of recovery technique isn't 'using more happily', it's 'no longer needing it'. Gotō wrote in the afterword to report 7: I no longer need dextromethorphan to maintain my life, and I've probably escaped the sigma plateau; even if I later try trihexyphenidyl to bring on memory recovery, I won't overdose.
You can pursue, not overdose; you can record, not sink. Recovery technique is a map for people who want to run, not a permit for people who want to stay.
